Writer Elizabeth Alexander on how she copes with fear

On Wild Card, famous guests answer questions that we don't always talk about. Writer Elizabeth Alexander talks about how she copes with fear.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Each week, a guest draws a card from NPR's Wild Card deck and answers a big question about their life. Elizabeth Alexander stopped writing poetry after she lost her husband, Ficre Ghebreyesus, in 2012. But she hasn't stopped writing altogether. Her new book, "Signals Across Vast Distances," is a collection of essays. Alexander talked to Wild Card host Rachel Martin about the lingering effects of her loss.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

RACHEL MARTIN: How big of a role does fear have in your life?

ELIZABETH ALEXANDER: Yeah. I've written about and have faced actual dying. But it was very - more than startling when it happened seemingly out of the blue with my husband a few days...

MARTIN: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: ...After his 50th birthday. I think there was a lot of fear after that that the earth was full of sinkholes.

MARTIN: Right. I would imagine that. I mean, when - it was so sudden. He died of cardiac arrest.

ALEXANDER: Yes.

MARTIN: And then your son.

ALEXANDER: Yes, and I write about that. You know...

MARTIN: He's fine, but...

ALEXANDER: He is so fine.

MARTIN: We should say that.

ALEXANDER: So with his permission...

MARTIN: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: ...I have written here about an absolutely mysterious heart attack that he had when he was 19 years old.

MARTIN: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: And that there are literally still scientists and doctors who are trying to figure out what happened. It was a medical mystery of that order. And so I think that, to what role does fear play, I don't feel that I can live with it all the time because it would be paralyzing.

MARTIN: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: Even just fear of accidents. You know, my sons are tall guys who love that game of basketball, which is a truly, truly great game, but someone is always hurt.

MARTIN: (Laughter).

ALEXANDER: Always. But I think also for them, I would not - because a cataclysmic thing happened to that 19-year-old, would I want fear to have him in a place where he didn't extend his body, where he didn't push it to the max...

MARTIN: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: ...Where he didn't take risks?

MARTIN: Yeah. How - your kids were how old when Ficre died?

ALEXANDER: Eleven and 12.

MARTIN: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: Yeah.

MARTIN: And so I imagine part of your job then is to just move beyond your own fear because you have these two humans.

ALEXANDER: Yes, yes. But it's sometimes challenging. My older son played football senior year in high school after my saying no football, no football, no football, which - I was afraid.

MARTIN: Yeah.

ALEXANDER: I thought, like, what if, you know, a terrible thing happens? And a parent friend of mine kind of knew what was animating that fear. And he said, just because that happened to their father, you don't want them to be afraid to trust their bodies.

MARTIN: Yeah. Yeah.

ALEXANDER: You know, and that was a great, loving call.

DETROW: You can watch Rachel Martin's full conversation with Elizabeth Alexander for NPR's Wild Card wherever you get your podcasts. Alexander's new book, "Signals Across Vast Distances: Essays And Tales," is out now.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

item.description:

Contrary to popular belief, foot traffic and spending at malls is up

This is the biggest shopping weekend for the American mall, which — despite widespread belief to the contrary — is not dying. One reason? Teens and tweens have rediscovered the hangout.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Today, the day after Thanksgiving, is the biggest shopping day of the year. It is a huge day for American malls. Now, you might be thinking, aren't shopping malls dying out? NPR's retail correspondent Alina Selyukh gets this question a lot.

ALINA SELYUKH, BYLINE: The idea of ailing malls comes up constantly. I was recently interviewing holiday shoppers in Manhattan, talking to cousins Chelsea Bates and Sawyer Hunley, visiting from Tennessee, and they brought it up.

CHELSEA BATES: Malls are just, I mean...

SAWYER HUNLEY: A dying thing.

BATES: Yeah, they kind of are a dying thing.

SELYUKH: And of course, like any conventional wisdom, there is truth to it. Lots of malls have died, says Michael Brown, who advises retailers at Carney Consulting.

MICHAEL BROWN: Some of them had to die.

SELYUKH: Because they were small, outdated, boring. But here's what's also happening. Shopping malls today are one of the most valuable property types of all commercial real estate. Last month, visits to indoor malls increased 4% from a year ago, according to foot traffic tracking firm Placer.ai. Visits to outdoor malls grew almost 6%.

BROWN: Malls are not dying. The moles are alive and prospering.

SELYUKH: Even if we're far from their heyday. That was in the '80s and the '90s, when any teenager would tell you it was the place to go. America had built so much retail space, more than any other country, and that became an expensive problem when people began to shop on the internet. Add to that the 2008 recession, then came the fallout from private equity buying up so many retailers, then the COVID pandemic. This long shake-up claimed legendary victims, like Sears and Toys "R" Us and Forever 21. The American Mall was gutted.

MOLLY MORGAN: I stopped coming, I think, a lot to do in part with the department stores closing.

SELYUKH: Molly Morgan is 37. She's visiting the mall of her youth, the Annapolis Mall in Maryland.

MORGAN: I remember all the - like, Lord Taylor closed, Nordstrom closed.

SELYUKH: But notice the part where she is back at the mall today. And the reason is her daughter, Nora Stickley.

NORA STICKLEY: I go every weekend.

SELYUKH: She's 12.

NORA: We went to the mall one day, and we really liked it, so we just kept coming back.

SELYUKH: The kids are rejuvenating the mall. And shopping with a crew of tweens is like navigating a tiny tornado with pocket money and hot takes.

NORA: Yeah. I would say...

IZABEL NASATKA: Everybody goes to the mall. It's, like, the main thing.

NORA: I don't think everybody goes to the mall. It's just really fun. And if you don't, you're a loser.

IZABEL: Ooh. Nora.

SELYUKH: Strong opinions.

The other voice is friend Izabel Nasatka, who's also 12. The shopping gang sweeps through Claire's, then a store called Rumilife, then one called BoxLunch. Every squishy (ph) gets squished, every plushy petted, every fidget toy rolled and clicked and flipped.

UNIDENTIFIED CHILD #1: Should I get this glitter baby?

UNIDENTIFIED CHILD #2: You should get it.

UNIDENTIFIED CHILD #3: Oh, my God, guys, they have squishy butter.

UNIDENTIFIED CHILD #1: Should I get the baby, though?

UNIDENTIFIED CHILD #2: You should get the baby, though.

SELYUKH: To survive into this new generation, malls had to take a long, hard look at themselves. Michael Brown, the retail consultant, once told me this quip that it wasn't malls that were dying. It was the lousy malls. He'd used a stronger word.

BROWN: When you want to buy something, you can buy it online. But that's just buying. Shopping is a completely different activity and social activity that people want to do.

SELYUKH: You have to have stuff besides stuff - maybe arcades or movies or a gym or cool claw machines and robots serving sushi - a reason for families to visit besides the stores.

IZABEL: Somebody's getting their ears pierced.

SELYUKH: Did you just give her a thumbs up?

NORA: Yeah. Got to hype everybody up.

SELYUKH: With the return of the youths, malls have had a mixed response. Some have cited rowdy behavior and enforced curfews or required chaperones. This mall, for now, is cool with the kids, and the parents say, it's a much nicer alternative to their other hangout, which is downtown. The mall is contained, enclosed and well-lit. Nasatka offers up this wisdom.

IZABEL: I mean, honestly, any place is just cool as long as you're, like, with cool people.

SELYUKH: This crew ends its epic mall odyssey at their favorite store, Hot Topic. They look at the wall of T-shirts and seem to know all the bands from decades before they were born. The adults joke that the '90s really are having a comeback, and the American mall is here for it. Alina Selyukh, NPR News.

item.description:

Last night my father called. He wants her legal assistance to clear his criminal record from the ’90s, back when I was a kid growing up in Las Vegas. His only run in with the law: an arrest for being the middleman in a cocaine deal. He didn’t technically buy the coke or sell it to anyone. No, not exactly. What he did was introduce the guy who sold it to a couple of other guys, and one of them was a police informant and, well, arrests were made. A short trial followed, and since all three men were Cuban immigrants, they were convicted of federal drug crimes. Each man had to serve prison time, including my father, of course.

The next morning was my long teaching day, but eventually, I did pick up the FaceTime. When my father asked for an update on my message to Kim, without hesitating, I lied and said I’d messaged her on Instagram to no response.

“She just has so many followers,” I said. “I didn’t expect her to answer.”

He groaned and nodded. My lie was good enough.

Then he asked about my brother and my mom in Florida and “her boring husband, João.” I assured him that everyone was fine, and then I asked him if he knew who Reinaldo Arenas was, since I’d just read his 1992 memoir, Before Night Falls. I told my father that Arenas, too, came here on the Mariel Boatlift in 1980, and that he’d written a famous memoir about growing up in Cuba as a gay man living under the Castro regime. But that, sadly, he’d died of an intentional overdose in 1990, after being diagnosed with AIDS and the physical deterioration that followed.

My father hadn’t heard of him. I didn’t expect him to be familiar with Arenas’s writing, since he doesn’t read very well, but I thought that maybe he knew of him, had possibly heard of him from the other refugees—even though 125,000 people migrated on those boats. My assumption might seem silly, but my father is the most charismatic man I’ve ever known. An enthralling storyteller. He would have made an excellent car salesman, or, in another life with some degrees and without the drug conviction, a wonderful litigator.

“How long was the boat ride from Havana?” I asked.

“Oof, about ten hours,” he said. “That boat was slower than a Russian movie.”

The boat was a shrimp boat and when it took off, people wanted to shout, to burst into celebratory howls, but everyone was told to be quiet until they had exited Cuban waters, about 12 miles away. So he and his brothers—Carlos, Papele (Jorge), Pedro, Domingo, Armando, and Eduardo (who succumbed to alcoholism before I could ever meet him)—watched as dolphins and other flying fish leapt through the air, a sight my father had never seen before. And once they reached mile 12, which took ages in the impossibly sluggish boat, my father couldn’t see his island anymore, and everyone was exhausted by then, so there was no cheering after all. No noise. Most of the other passengers had dozed off, and in that unanticipated moment of stillness, my father was suddenly overcome with a deep melancholy, “a tristeza,” he called it, silently watching his home disappear into nothing. At age twenty-nine, it was the first time my father had ever left his island. In the end, the 90-mile journey to South Florida took ten whole hours.

Once the boat landed, there was no big welcome. The truth is some Americans didn’t want them here, and neither did some of the Cubans who were already here. Unlike the more affluent, lighter-skinned Cubans who’d arrived in the US during the earlier waves of immigration, the Marielitos were browner and blacker and gayer and poorer.

The year of the boatlift, because tensions on the island had come to a boil and citizens were causing too much of a ruckus—you know, because of typical dictatorship things like political repression, no free speech, hunger, etc.—Castro finally opened the port of Mariel and granted everyone permission to leave. “Escoria,” the fleeing refugees were labeled by the regime. Scum. Then President Jimmy Carter reluctantly gave his blessing and, like many others, my father gave both his sisters a long hug goodbye and headed north in search of something else, something new, something, anything, a little more free.

***

It’s almost the end of the semester now and my father won’t stop blowing up my phone. Calling twice, sometimes three times a day. The calls might be due to the season: Christmas is next week. After getting so used to years of his absence—once he’d moved out in my teens to start a new family with the next door neighbor—I now chalk up these recent calls to old age, a form of restitution, I suppose. The stuff we humans do when we get closer to kicking the bucket. Maybe he’s also calling because of the cooler weather. He’s not working these days. He’s looking for a new job, at age seventy-three, after losing his social security benefits. All because he never fixed his legal problems after the old drug conviction. His retirement money from his various service jobs at the casinos on the Las Vegas strip did come in for a couple of years, in small, monthly paychecks, but then the government stopped it abruptly. He and his wife (the neighbor) say they can’t afford to pay for a lawyer’s help. This means that he’s currently on deportation status. For now, he has to schedule yearly appointments to check in with ICE, at the Non-Detained Office on Las Vegas Blvd. There, an agent makes sure his home address hasn’t changed and that all his personal information is updated in their system. The agent briefly glances at his face and signs some papers to confirm he hasn’t been up to any nefarious crap, then sends him on his way.…

One summer I dated a street performer who painted her entire body gold and stood, still as a statue, on a milk crate outside Jackson Square. My gig as a day-shift bartender was lucrative in comparison. I visited her during my breaks. She never moved, so I lingered off to the side, smoking and hoping she noticed me standing there. The statue of Andrew Jackson loomed behind us, tourists posing for photos underneath him. At night she’d scrub off the paint, but it never fully came off. There were always little flecks of gold stuck between her teeth or haloing her hairline. As she changed out of her gold vest and gold tie, I’d tell her about my day, how I sold daiquiris to old men who flirted with me despite my buzz cut and bridge piercing. Even though I needed the tips, I couldn’t rouse the energy to flirt back. That was the difference between her and me, she said. She was a performer. She left gold smears on the edge of my bathtub, on the cups in the kitchen. When I kissed her, it tasted like arts and crafts. Her washable paint, skin-safe. That carnival smell of powdered sugar and sweat and honest summer fun. When drunk, she had a bad habit of leaning out my window and inviting people in the street up to do shots. She’d complain to anyone who’d listen about how bad business was these days, how she was this close to leaving the city for good. We supported each other’s vices: I’d bring her discounted liquor, and she gave me the cigarettes people dropped into her bucket. I carried an Altoids tin with my mismatched collection, Camels and Newports and American Spirits lined up like toy soldiers. While she sat in front of the mirror, I realized I hadn’t touched a paintbrush in six years. It used to be all I could think about: going to art school, making a name for myself, working until my hands bled. I watched her use a fat makeup brush to pack paint into the webs between her fingers. I wondered aloud why anyone came to see her work when they could walk twenty feet and see a real statue—ten times her size, a real effigy of a rotten man on his horse, rearing toward the next atrocity. She looked at me like I couldn’t possibly understand. A few weeks later, she made good on her promise and left the city. I don’t know if she ever came back. The day she left, I came home to find that she had scrubbed every inch of my apartment. The paint smears on the cupboards, the grains of glitter in the sink, all gone. Even the grout between the bathroom tiles was spotless. I looked down at my reflection on the white countertop. It was every color but gold.
